system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted after an MRI revealed a new right portal vein thrombosis. He was asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. He was started on intravenous heparin and transitioned to warfarin, achieving a therapeutic INR of 2.7 by discharge. A transient rise in creatinine, likely due to contrast from a CT scan, resolved with adjustment of his diuretic regimen. His pleural effusion showed improvement, and he remained free of infection or bleeding complications. He was discharged home with warfarin for at least three months, continued management of cirrhosis and HCC, and new prescriptions for inhalers as part of his transplant evaluation, with outpatient follow-up planned for INR monitoring and a bubble echocardiogram.
problems: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. I understand you were confused earlier today. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better, actually. I woke up not knowing where I was, and I was really agitated. My wife said I didn’t make sense. But now I feel like myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Based on your history, this sounds like hepatic encephalopathy—confusion caused by your liver not filtering toxins well. You’ve had episodes before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, maybe once or twice a year. But lately, it’s been happening almost every week. I’ve been taking lactulose three times a day, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, your dose was recently increased. You were on 15 ml three times a day, but now it’s 30 ml. That’s to help prevent these episodes by clearing out toxins through more bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it was increased. I’ve been taking the same amount. Should I be having more bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the goal is about 3 to 4 soft bowel movements per day. If you start feeling confused again, you can take a dose every two hours until you feel better—just don’t exceed 6 doses in 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about my liver? Is something new going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound and a CT scan tonight. Your liver disease is stable—no new tumors. The treated areas look unchanged, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood clot in my portal vein? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The clot in the right portal vein is still there, but it hasn’t gotten worse. It’s stable compared to your last scan. That’s why we’re keeping you on warfarin—to prevent it from growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about it spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The main and left portal veins are still open, and there’s no sign of new shunts that could worsen your encephalopathy. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. Your liver enzymes and kidney function are stable. Sodium is a bit low, but that’s common with cirrhosis and not concerning right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts? I remember they were low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cells and platelets are low, which is expected with your liver disease and spleen enlargement. But they haven’t dropped further, so we’re not worried about infection or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re back to your baseline, and all the tests show stability. We’ll keep your lactulose at 30 ml three times a day and continue rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin? Do I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same dose—3 mg daily. You’ll need weekly INR checks at first to make sure it’s in the right range. Your primary care team will manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel confused again, increase your lactulose as we discussed. Also watch for fever, belly swelling, or weight gain—more than 3 pounds in 3 days. Call your doctor if that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? I didn’t take my glyburide today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it in the hospital because your blood sugar was high, but not dangerously so. You can restart it at home. Just keep an eye on your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my next appointment with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s already scheduled. You’ll see him for your regular HCC and liver monitoring, including an EGD soon to check your varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ll follow up and keep taking my meds as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re doing well—just stay on top of the lactulose and the INR checks. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re feeling clear-headed, no dizziness or weakness? All set to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel fine. Ready to go home and rest.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for altered mental status due to hepatic encephalopathy. He had experienced increasing frequency of encephalopathy episodes over recent weeks. Upon admission, he was confused but improved rapidly with lactulose. Imaging showed stable portal vein thrombosis and no new liver lesions or portosystemic shunts. His lactulose dose was increased to 30 ml three times daily to achieve 3–4 bowel movements per day, and he remained on rifaximin, warfarin, and other home medications. Labs showed stable liver and kidney function with mild hyponatremia and pancytopenia consistent with cirrhosis. He was discharged home the same day with instructions to monitor for recurrent confusion, weight gain, or infection, and to continue outpatient follow-up with hepatology and INR monitoring.
